input.step_by_step_reasoning: 1) Inventory: the World Model has 13 entities and 12 visual_connections. 2) Node normalization: the 'User' actor uses the service type 'User', which is not in the vocabulary. The user reaches the system through a web browser or a mobile app, so it maps to UserConsumerWebMobile. It is kept as the system entry point because ledger edges must keep their endpoints. CSV & XL, the Angular Front End and the Python Back End are mapped to ThirdParty. 3) Fusion: the two OpenSearch icons are one logical OpenSearch cluster on Graviton2. The ingestion Lambda loads data into it and the Back End queries it as 'the data layer', so they are fused into one node. All ledger edges stay attached to the fused node. The three S3 icons are kept separate because they do distinct jobs: raw upload, the validated copy (a different folder), and large report storage. The two Lambdas are also kept separate: one validates and one processes and ingests. 4) Flows: Flow 0 is ingestion (CSV/XL -> raw S3 -> validation Lambda by S3 event trigger -> validated S3 -> processing Lambda by trigger -> OpenSearch). Flow 1 is retrieval: the web path is User -> FE -> User, then User -> BE. Mobile requests go straight to BE. BE then queries OpenSearch and, in parallel, RDS, and responds to the User. The ledger has only one User->BE arrow, so it covers both the web and mobile entry. Flow 2 is large reports (>10,000 records): BE uploads the report to the reports S3 bucket, then sends a notice through SES to the User, who downloads it from S3 using a pre-signed URL. 5) Non-ledger edges added because the audio explicitly states them: Back End -> SES ('send an intimation to the user via SES'), SES -> User, and S3 (Reports) -> User (pre-signed URL download). The SES edges stop SES from being an orphan node. 6) Self-check: 12 visual_connections entries and 15 edges emitted (12 ledger + 3 from the audio). 15 >= 12.

graph.name: Cybex Trade Data Processing and Retrieval with Amazon OpenSearch (Novantec)
graph.categories: Analytics, Search, Event-Driven, Serverless, Data Processing
graph.notes: Event-driven ingestion of import/export trade data from CSV/Excel into an Amazon OpenSearch cluster running on Graviton2. The system started with 1.5 billion records and has grown more than 3.5x to about 5 billion. Reports with 15-20 complex parameters return in 2-4 seconds. Graviton2 saves about 25-30% of operating cost (about $100K). Retrieval works through an Angular web front end or a mobile app via a Python back end. Large reports (>10,000 records) are stored in S3 and delivered by an SES email with a pre-signed URL.

nodes.name: CSV & XL
nodes.notes: Raw import/export trade data source files in CSV or Excel format. Started at about 1.5 billion records and has grown to about 5 billion (more than 3.5x).

nodes.name: Amazon S3 (Raw Data)
nodes.notes: S3 bucket that receives the uploaded raw CSV/Excel files. Upload events trigger the validation Lambda.

nodes.name: AWS Lambda (Validation)
nodes.notes: Triggered by the raw upload. Validates the data and highlights any discrepancies. If the data is valid, it copies it to a separate validated folder in S3.

nodes.name: Amazon S3 (Validated Data)
nodes.notes: Separate folder in the S3 buckets that holds the validated data copy. Triggers the processing Lambda.

nodes.name: AWS Lambda (Processing)
nodes.notes: Triggered when the validated copy lands. Processes the validated data and ingests it into the OpenSearch cluster.

nodes.name: Amazon OpenSearch Cluster (Graviton2)
nodes.notes: The two drawn OpenSearch icons (ingestion and retrieval) are fused into one cluster. Runs on Graviton2 instances, saving about 25-30% of operating cost (about $100K). Uses query templates mapped to relevant indexes and the OpenSearch analyzer to fine-tune queries. An aggregated layer on top of the processed data serves complex reports such as trend analysis. Serves reports with 15-20 complex parameters in 2-4 seconds over about 5 billion records.

nodes.name: User (Web Browser / Mobile App)
nodes.notes: End customer who reaches the data from anywhere at any time, either through the web application in a browser or through the mobile application.

nodes.name: Front End (Angular)
nodes.notes: Web front-end application built with Angular. Web browser requests go here first.

nodes.name: Back End (Python)
nodes.notes: Back-end application built with Python. Receives requests from the web app and directly from mobile apps, queries the data layer, and sends responses back to the user. Generates large reports (>10,000 records).

nodes.name: Amazon RDS
nodes.notes: Relational database in the retrieval data layer, queried by the back end. Not described in the audio.

nodes.name: Amazon S3 (Reports)
nodes.notes: Stores generated reports with more than 10,000 records. Users download them through a pre-signed URL, which is good for security.

nodes.name: Amazon SES
nodes.notes: Sends an email to the user with a pre-signed URL to download the large report from S3.

edges.notes: Raw CSV/Excel data files are uploaded into the S3 bucket.
The upload event triggers the Lambda that validates the data.
If there are no discrepancies, a copy of the validated data is uploaded to a different folder in the S3 buckets.
The validated copy triggers the processing Lambda.
The processed validated data is ingested into the OpenSearch cluster (query templates, index mapping, aggregated layer).
Web app path: the user sends a request to the Angular front end through the web browser.
The front end responds back to the user's browser.
The request reaches the Python back end, either from the web browser or directly from the mobile app.
The back end queries the data layer (OpenSearch). Reports with 15-20 parameters return in 2-4 seconds.
The back end queries the RDS database, which is part of the data layer.
The response is sent back to the user through the back end application.
Reports with more than 10,000 records are uploaded to the S3 bucket.
The back end has SES send a notice to the user (stated in the audio, not drawn).
SES emails the user a pre-signed URL to download the report (stated in the audio, not drawn).
The user downloads the large report from S3 through the pre-signed URL (stated in the audio, not drawn).
